source: Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel, chapter 2, The Save the Cat! Beat Sheet

sizes.single: A single-scene beat. One scene or one chapter: one piece of information.
sizes.multi: A multi-scene beat. It spans several scenes or chapters.

pattern: The beats come in pairs of action and reaction. A single-scene beat is an action, a hinge the story turns on. The multi-scene beat after it is the reaction, the stretch where the hero lives with what just happened. The Catalyst is followed by the Debate; the All Is Lost is another Catalyst, and the Dark Night of the Soul is another Debate. Inside the Finale, the High Tower Surprise and Dig Deep Down repeat the pair once more.

opening_image.does: A quick before snapshot of the hero and the hero's world.
teach: It is an image, so show it. Open on the hero doing something, with one or two of their flaws visibly making a mess of their life. It is not an opening inner monologue, and it is not an info dump.
It also tells the reader what kind of book this is: its tone, its style, the ride they are about to take.
It is a mirror beat. The Final Image is its opposite, the after picture. The further apart the two pictures are, the more the journey was worth taking.
checklist: Is it one scene or one chapter?
Is it visual: are you showing, not telling?
Is at least one of the hero's flaws on display?

theme_stated.does: Someone hints at what the hero will learn by the end: their life lesson, their need.
teach: Usually a secondary character says it, often in passing, and the story moves on. It is planted, not preached: no billboards, no five pages on it.
The hero ignores it. At the start the hero resists change, so they dismiss the person who says it. That is why it works best coming from someone the hero would believably wave off.
It does not have to be spoken by a person. A sign, a book, a line on a screen can carry it, as long as it points at the hero's need.
checklist: Does the theme relate directly to the hero's need, their life lesson?
Is it stated by someone, or something, other than the hero?
Can the hero easily and believably dismiss it?

setup.goes: 1% to 10%: the first tenth of the book.
setup.does: Shows the hero's world before everything changes: who they are, what they want, and what is wrong.
teach: Set up the hero and a goal they are actively chasing. That goal is their want, not their need, so it will not really fix their life.
Introduce the A Story characters, the people of the status quo world.
Show the hero's flaws in more than one part of life: at home, at work, at play. A flaw that shows up everywhere is a flaw the reader believes.
List the things that need fixing. They come back later as checkpoints: if none of them change as the book goes on, the hero is not being transformed enough.
Somewhere in the Setup, the stasis = death moment makes it clear that staying put is not an option. Something has to happen.
checklist: Have you shown at least one thing that needs fixing?
Have you introduced at least one A Story character?
Is the hero's want, their external goal, clear?
Is the hero shown in more than one area of life?
Is there a sense that change is urgent (stasis = death)?

stasis_death.goes: Inside the Setup, just before the Catalyst.
stasis_death.does: The moment that shows the hero cannot stay as they are.
teach: This is a moment inside the Setup, not a beat of its own, so it has no size of its own. It takes its room from the Setup.

catalyst.does: Something happens to the hero that sends their life in a new direction.
teach: It happens to the hero. It is an action, something that busts through the status quo, not a quiet realization.
It often arrives as bad news, because people rarely change until something bad makes them.
Make it big. The test: could the hero easily go back to their normal life tomorrow? If yes, the Catalyst is not big enough. The reader should think: how will they ever recover from that?
checklist: Does the Catalyst happen to the hero?
Is it an action beat, with no revelations?
Is it big enough to break the status quo?
Is it impossible for the hero to go back to their normal life?

debate.goes: 10% to 20%: from the Catalyst to the end of Act 1.
debate.does: Shows how resistant the hero is to change, or prepares them for the break into Act 2.
teach: It is a reaction beat, and it usually takes the shape of a question: what do I do now? Nobody accepts change right away, and a hero who does loses credibility.
Show the hero struggling with it in more than one part of life: home, work, play.
Sometimes the decision is obvious, and the Debate is preparation instead: training, packing, steeling themselves. Then the question becomes: I know I am going, but am I ready?
checklist: Can you sum up the Debate as a question, or, for a preparation Debate, say what the hero is preparing for and why?
Is there a real sense of hesitation?
Is the hero shown debating in more than one area of life?

break_into_two.does: The hero leaves the old world and old way of thinking and steps into a new one.
teach: Act 2 is the upside-down version of Act 1, so the break should be clear: we are not in Kansas anymore. The journey can be literal or a new way of living.
The hero chooses it. Someone may offer the door, but the hero walks through it. This is where every hero proves there is something in them worth rooting for.
They are still chasing their want, so this is fixing things the wrong way: a bandage over the wound, not real healing. Break into Three is its mirror, where they fix things the right way.
checklist: Is the hero leaving an old world and entering a new one, or trying something new?
Is Act 2 the opposite of Act 1?
Is the break clear and distinct?
Does the hero make a proactive choice?
Is the choice driven by the want, and can you say why it is the wrong way to change?

b_story.goes: 22%, usually right after the Break into Two; always within the first 25%.
b_story.does: Introduces the character who will help the hero learn the theme.
teach: The single-scene beat is the introduction. The B Story character then appears through the rest of Act 2 and often Act 3, and that longer thread is a storyline of its own.
Two tests: they belong to the upside-down Act 2 world, someone the hero would not have met or noticed in Act 1; and they help guide the hero toward the life lesson.
They can be a love interest, a friend, a mentor, even a nemesis. They can embody the theme, bring it out by their nature, or mirror the hero's flaw in an exaggerated form.
There can be two, a twin B story, as long as each guides the hero in a different way.
checklist: Have you introduced a new love interest, mentor, friend or nemesis?
Can you say how this character represents the theme?
Is the character a product of the upside-down Act 2 world?

fun_and_games.goes: 20% to 50%: the whole first half of Act 2.
fun_and_games.does: Delivers the promise of the premise: the hero either shines or flounders in the new world.
teach: This is the part the reader picked the book up for. Fun is for the reader, not necessarily for the hero.
Vary it: up, down, up, down. It is sometimes called the bouncing ball. A win, then a loss, a breakthrough, then a false lead.
Underneath the bouncing there is one overall direction, an upward path or a downward path. Choose it, because it decides the Midpoint and the rest of Act 2.
checklist: Is the hero clearly floundering or succeeding in the new world?
Does it deliver on the promise of the premise?
Does it show how Act 2 is the upside-down version of Act 1?

midpoint.does: Marks the middle with a false victory or a false defeat, while raising the stakes.
teach: Three things happen here: a false victory or a false defeat; the stakes are raised; the A and B stories cross.
An upward Fun and Games leads to a false victory, a downward one to a false defeat. Either way it is false, because the hero still has not learned the theme.
Ways to raise the stakes: a love story ramps up, a ticking clock appears, a game-changing twist lands, or a big party or celebration puts the new self on public view.
Here the story begins to shift from the want to the need, and it becomes harder than ever for the hero to go back.
checklist: Can you name a false victory or a false defeat?
Have the stakes been raised?
Do the A and B stories cross?
Is there a shift from the want toward the need?

bad_guys_close_in.goes: 50% to 75%: often the longest beat in the book.
bad_guys_close_in.does: Things get steadily worse after a false victory, or better after a false defeat, while the internal bad guys keep working.
teach: Its direction is the opposite of the Fun and Games. After a false victory, things go downhill; after a false defeat, they climb.
There do not have to be literal villains. Every story has internal bad guys: the hero's own flaws, still sabotaging them because the theme has not been learned.
checklist: Does this beat run opposite to the Fun and Games?
Have you shown how the internal bad guys, the flaws, work against the hero?

teach: Something happens to the hero that knocks them deep into defeat. Make it bigger than the Catalyst; they must be worse off than when the book began. A timid All Is Lost makes the final change feel contrived.
The whiff of death: someone dies or nearly dies, or something ends. The old world, the old self, the old way of thinking dies here so a new one can be born.
The hero is in some way responsible, even if they did not cause the event. Without responsibility there is no lesson.
It works like another Catalyst: the first pushed the hero into the Debate, this one pushes them into the Dark Night of the Soul.
checklist: Does something happen to the hero?
Is it big enough to push the hero into Act 3?
Is there a whiff of death?
Does it feel like another Catalyst?

dark_night.goes: 75% to 80%: to the end of Act 2.
dark_night.does: How the hero reacts to the All Is Lost, and how they break through to a resolution.
teach: It is another Debate. The All Is Lost lasted one scene; now the hero needs time to process it, which is why this beat gets several scenes or chapters. It is sometimes called the wallowing beat. Not every hero wallows: some rage, some deny.
It is the darkness before the dawn. Something deep inside is working, and it ends in the Dark Night epiphany, where the hero sees the truth in a new light.
It often revolves around a question, like the Debate did.
It is the one beat where the hero may move backward: the return to the familiar. Going home shows how much they have changed, because home no longer fits.
checklist: Is the hero reflecting on something here?
Is this beat leading the hero toward an epiphany?
Does the hero's life seem worse off than at the beginning?

break_into_three.does: The hero realizes what they must do to fix the problems they caused, and to fix themselves.
teach: The hero finally faces the truth: I am flawed, but now that I know that, I can fix it. They learn the theme.
The mirror of the Break into Two. That was fixing things the wrong way, for the want; this is fixing them the right way, for the need.
One scene or chapter. It can be done in a page, even a paragraph.
checklist: Does the hero learn the universal lesson, the theme, here?
Does the hero make a proactive decision to fix something?
Is the decision based on what the hero needs, and can you say why it is the right way to change?

finale.does: The hero proves they have learned the theme and acts on it.
teach: Act 3 is the synthesis: the hero blends who they were in Act 1 with what they learned in Act 2. The A and B stories intertwine.

The Five-Point Finale gives the long beat road markers: gathering the team, executing the plan, the High Tower Surprise, dig deep down, and executing the new plan. The High Tower Surprise is yet another Catalyst; Dig Deep Down is yet another Debate.
Make the hero work for it. A finale with no struggle reads as too easy.
checklist: Is Act 3 a synthesis of Act 1 and Act 2?
Does the hero struggle to enact the plan?
Is there a Dig Deep Down moment that proves the theme is learned?
Do the A and B stories intertwine?

final_image.goes: 99% to 100%: the last scene or chapter.
final_image.does: An after snapshot that shows how much the hero has changed.
teach: The mirror of the Opening Image. If the two pictures are not starkly different, rethink the beats: the distance between them is the proof the journey mattered.
Like the Opening Image, show it, as an image.
checklist: Is it one scene, or a set of closely connected ones?
Is it visual?
Is the hero's transformation evident?
Does the after picture mirror the before picture?
